questions.question: Consider a 5-stage pipelined processor with Instruction Fetch (IF), Instruction Decode (ID), Execute (EX), Memory Access (MEM), and Register Writeback (WB) stages. Which of the following statements about forwarding is/are CORRECT?

options.A:
In a pipelined execution, forwarding means the result from a source stage of an
earlier instruction is passed on to the destination stage of a later instruction
options.B:
In forwarding, data from the output of the MEM stage can be passed on to the
input of the EX stage of the next instruction
options.C: Forwarding cannot prevent all pipeline stalls
options.D:
Forwarding does not require any extra hardware to retrieve the data from the
pipeline stages

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- Option 1: this is exactly the definition of forwarding (bypassing) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Option 2: a value available at the output of MEM (e.g. a loaded value) can be fed to the EX input of a later instruction [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Option 3: forwarding cannot remove every stall. Example: load followed immediately by an instruction using the loaded value still needs 1 stall (load-use hazard) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Option 4: forwarding needs extra hardware (extra paths, multiplexers, hazard detection logic) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: Options 1, 2 and 3

questions.question:
The following are some events that occur after a device controller issues an interrupt while process L is under execution.
(P) The processor pushes the process status of L onto the control stack.
(Q) The processor finishes the execution of the current instruction.
(R) The processor executes the interrupt service routine.
(S) The processor pops the process status of L from the control stack.
(T) The processor loads the new PC value based on the interrupt.
Which one of the following is the correct order in which the events above occur?
questions.explanation:
Order of interrupt handling:
Q: finish the current instruction [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] P: save L's status on the stack [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] T: load the PC with the ISR address [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] R: run the ISR [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] S: restore L's status.

Answer: QPTRS

questions.question: Which one of the following statements is FALSE?

options.A:
In the cycle stealing mode of DMA, one word of data is transferred between an I/O
device and main memory in a stolen cycle
options.B:
For bulk data transfer, the burst mode of DMA has a higher throughput than the
cycle stealing mode
options.C:
Programmed I/O mechanism has a better CPU utilization than the interrupt driven
I/O mechanism
options.D:
The CPU can start executing an interrupt service routine faster with vectored
interrupts than with non-vectored interrupts

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- Cycle stealing: DMA takes one bus cycle and moves one word [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Burst mode keeps the bus for the whole block (no repeated bus requests), so it has higher throughput for bulk transfer [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Programmed I/O has better CPU utilization than interrupt-driven I/O [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE. In programmed I/O the CPU keeps polling the device status and wastes cycles; interrupt-driven I/O lets the CPU do other work until the device interrupts.
- Vectored interrupts give the ISR address directly (no polling to find the device), so ISR starts faster [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: Programmed I/O has better CPU utilization than interrupt driven I/O (FALSE)

questions.question: A computer has a memory hierarchy consisting of two-level cache (L1 and L2) and a main memory. If the processor needs to access data from memory, it first looks into L1 cache. If the data is not found in L1 cache, it goes to L2 cache. If it fails to get the data from L2 cache, it goes to main memory, where the data is definitely available. Hit rates and access times of various memory units are shown in the figure. The average memory access time in nanoseconds (ns) is _________. (rounded off to two decimal places)
questions.explanation:
This system uses hierarchical (serial) cache access: to reach L2, the processor must have already tried and missed in L1; to reach main memory, it must have already tried and missed in both L1 and L2. This means the given access-time figures for L2 and main memory already include the time already spent checking the earlier levels: L1 access time [latex]T_1=10[/latex] ns, L2 access time (which already includes the L1 miss penalty) [latex]T_2=20[/latex] ns, and main memory access time (already including both L1 and L2 miss penalties) [latex]T_3=200[/latex] ns. Hit rates: [latex]H_1=0.95[/latex] (L1), [latex]H_2=0.85[/latex] (L2).

The average memory access time is a weighted sum over the three possible outcomes — hit in L1, miss-L1-then-hit-L2, or miss-both-then-go-to-memory:
[latex]\text{AMAT}=H_1T_1+(1-H_1)H_2T_2+(1-H_1)(1-H_2)T_3[/latex]
[latex]=0.95(10)+0.05(0.85)(20)+0.05(0.15)(200)[/latex]
[latex]=9.5+0.85+1.5=11.85[/latex] ns.

Answer: 11.85

questions.question:
The instruction pipeline of a RISC processor has the following stages: Instruction Fetch (IF), Instruction Decode (ID), Operand Fetch (OF), Perform Operation (PO) and Writeback (WB). The IF, ID, OF and WB stages take 1 clock cycle each for every instruction. Consider a sequence of 100 instructions. In the PO stage, 40 instructions take 3 clock cycles each, 35 instructions take 2 clock cycles each, and the remaining 25 instructions take 1 clock cycle each. Assume that there are no data hazards and no control hazards.
The number of clock cycles required for completion of execution of the sequence of instructions is ______.
questions.explanation:
The PO stage is the bottleneck, so the instructions flow through it back to back.
Total PO time = 40 [latex]\times[/latex] 3 + 35 [latex]\times[/latex] 2 + 25 [latex]\times[/latex] 1 = 215 cycles.

Add 3 cycles before the first PO (IF, ID, OF) and 1 after the last (WB): 3 + 215 + 1 = 219

Answer: 219

questions.question: Consider a disk pack with a seek time of 4 milliseconds and rotational speed of 10000 rotations per minute (RPM). It has 600 sectors per track and each sector can store 512 bytes of data. Consider a file stored in the disk. The file contains 2000 sectors. Assume that every sector access necessitates a seek, and the average rotational latency for accessing each sector is half of the time for one complete rotation. The total time (in milliseconds) needed to read the entire file is ____________.
questions.explanation:
One rotation = 60 / 10000 s = 6 ms.

Per sector: seek 4 + latency 3 + transfer 6/600 = 0.01 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 7.01 ms

Total = 2000 [latex]\times[/latex] 7.01 = 14020 ms

Answer: 14020

questions.question: A certain processor deploys a single-level cache. The cache block size is 8 words and the word size is 4 bytes. The memory system uses a 60-MHz clock. To service a cache-miss, the memory controller first takes 1 cycle to accept the starting address of the block, it then takes 3 cycles to fetch all the eight words of the block, and finally transmits the words of the requested block at the rate of 1 word per cycle. The maximum bandwidth for the memory system when the program running on the processor issues a series of read operations is _________[latex]\times 10^6[/latex] bytes/sec.
questions.explanation:
One cache miss brings one block of 8 words [latex]\times[/latex] 4 bytes = 32 bytes.
Cycles per block = 1 (address) + 3 (fetch) + 8 (transfer, 1 word per cycle) = 12 cycles.

Time per block = 12 / 60 MHz = 0.2 [latex]\mu[/latex]s.
Bandwidth = 32 bytes / 0.2 [latex]\mu[/latex]s = [latex]160\times10^6[/latex] bytes/s

Answer: 160

questions.question:
An access sequence of cache block addresses is of length N and contains n unique block
addresses. The number of unique block addresses between two consecutive accesses to the
same block address is bounded above K. What is the miss ratio if the access sequence is
passed through a cache of associativity A[latex]\geq[/latex]k exercising least-recently-used replacement policy?
questions.explanation:
Between two uses of the same block, at most k other blocks are used, and the cache holds A [latex]\ge[/latex] k blocks per set with LRU. So a block is never evicted before it is used again: only the first access to each of the n distinct blocks misses.

Miss ratio = n / N

Answer: n/N

questions.question:
An 8KB direct mapped write-back cache is organized as multiple blocks, each of
size 32-bytes. The processor generates 32-bit addresses. The cache controller
maintains the tag information for each cache block comprising of the following.
1 Valid bit
1 Modified bit
As many bits as the minimum needed to identify the memory block mapped in
the cache.
What is the total size of memory needed at the cache controller to store metadata
(tags) for the cache?

Checking each statement:
- Blocks = 8 KB / 32 B = 256 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] index = 8 bits, offset = 5 bits
- Tag = 32 [latex]-[/latex] 8 [latex]-[/latex] 5 = 19 bits
- Per block: 19 + 1 (valid) + 1 (modified) = 21 bits

Total = 256 [latex]\times[/latex] 21 = 5376 bits

Answer: 5376 bits

questions.question:
Consider a hard disk with 16 recording surfaces (0-15) having 16384 cylinders (0-16383) and each
cylinder contains 64 sectors (0-63). Data storage capacity in each sector is 512 bytes. Data are
organized cylinder-wise and the addressing format is (cylinder no., surface no., sector no.). A file
of size 42797 KB is stored in the disk and the starting disk location of the file is (1200, 9, 40).
What is the cylinder number of the last sector of the file, if it is stored in a contiguous manner?
questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- Sectors per cylinder = 16 [latex]\times[/latex] 64 = 1024
- File = 42797 KB / 0.5 KB = 85594 sectors
- Start (1200, 9, 40) is sector 9 [latex]\times[/latex] 64 + 40 = 616 of cylinder 1200, leaving 1024 [latex]-[/latex] 616 = 408 sectors there
- Remaining = 85594 [latex]-[/latex] 408 = 85186 = 83 full cylinders (1201-1283) + 194 sectors

The last sector is in cylinder 1284.

Answer: 1284

questions.question:
A processor uses a 32-bit instruction format and supports byte-addressable memory access. The ISA of the processor has 150 distinct instructions. The instructions are equally divided into two types, namely R-type and I-type, whose formats are shown below.

In the OPCODE, 1 bit is used to distinguish between I-type and R-type instructions and the remaining bits indicate the operation. The processor has 50 architectural registers, and all register fields in the instructions are of equal size.
Let X be the number of bits used to encode the UNUSED field, Y be the number of bits used to encode the OPCODE field, and Z be the number of bits used to encode the immediate value/address field. The value of X + 2Y + Z is ______
questions.explanation:
Find each field size:
- 150 instructions, 75 of each type. 1 bit for type + [latex]\lceil\log_2 75\rceil=7[/latex] bits [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Y = 8.
- 50 registers [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]\lceil\log_2 50\rceil=6[/latex] bits per register field.
- R-type: [latex]8+X+3\times6=32\Rightarrow[/latex] X = 6.
- I-type: [latex]8+2\times6+Z=32\Rightarrow[/latex] Z = 12.

[latex]X+2Y+Z=6+16+12=34[/latex]

Answer: 34

questions.question:
Consider a pipelined processor with 5 stages, Instruction Fetch(IF), Instruction Decode(ID), Execute (EX), Memory Access (MEM), and Write Back (WB). Each stage of the pipeline, except the EX stage, takes one cycle. Assume that the ID stage merely decodes the instruction and the register read is performed in the EX stage. The EX stage takes one cycle for ADD instruction and the register read is performed in the EX stage, The EX stage takes one cycle for ADD instruction and two cycles for MUL instruction. Ignore pipeline register latencies.
Consider the following sequence of 8 instructions:

ADD, MUL, ADD, MUL, ADD, MUL, ADD, MUL

Assume that every MUL instruction is data-dependent on the ADD instruction just before it and every ADD instruction (except the first ADD) is data-dependent on the MUL instruction just before it. The speedup defined as follows.

[latex]\textit{Speedup} = \dfrac{\text{Execution time without operand forwarding}}{\text{Execution time with operand forearding}}[/latex]

The Speedup achieved in executing the given instruction sequence on the pipelined processor (rounded to 2 decimal places) is _____________
questions.explanation:
Each instruction depends on the one before it. ADD uses EX for 1 cycle, MUL for 2.

With forwarding: the EX stages run back to back: 4 [latex]\times[/latex] (1 + 2) = 12 EX cycles from cycle 3 to 14, then MEM and WB [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 16 cycles.

Without forwarding: each instruction's EX (register read) waits until the previous one's WB. Each ADD/MUL pair then takes 1 + 2 EX cycles plus 2 waiting cycles (MEM, WB) each [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] the last WB is at cycle 30.

Speedup = 30 / 16 = 1.875 [latex]\approx[/latex] 1.87

Answer: 1.87

questions.question:
A 4 kilobyte (KB) byte-addressable memory is realized using four 1 KB memory blocks. Two input address lines (IA4 and IA3) are connected to the chip select (CS) port of these memory blocks through a decoder as shown in the figure. The remaining ten input address lines from IA11-IA0 are connected to the address port of these blocks. The chip select (CS) is active high.
